6.	Presents factual evidence as to why any man or group of men are granted postponement of military training in any plant or industry.
7.	Gives mobilization boards information helpful in deciding on application for postponement of military training to individuals or groups in any given plant or industry.
8.	Brings to the attention of the divisional registrars those men who may be delinquent or who have not notified their registrar of any change of addTess and for whom they are looking.
9.	Indicates to employment service any surplus labour.
10.	It has the approval and cooperation of both management and labour.
Conscientious objectors. Up to March 31, 1944, mobilization boards had given deferments to 8,932 conscientious objectors. Subsequently, 245 offered their services to the armed forces and were accepted as combatant soldiers or air force personnel. One hundred and twenty-two others have enlisted as non-combatant soldiers in the medical and dental corps.
The great majority of conscientious objectors have been quite willing to undertake alternative service work as directed. As at March 31, 1944, some 3,188 have been placed in agriculture under alternative service employment agreements, and 1,295 contracted [DOT] in non-agricultural employment. A number have been placed in hospitals as orderlies or have been sent to employment wThere conditions have made it difficult for employment offices to supply workers.
Wartime labour relations regulations. Recently I tabled in this house order in council P. C. 1003, known as the wartime labour relations regulations. These regulations will, I hope, mark a milestone in the history of labour legislation in Canada and contribute to a reduction of time lost through industrial disputes and to sound industrial relations generally.
It is very gratifying to note the warm reception the order has received both from representatives of the employers and of the workers and I should like to express my appreciation of the cooperation of the provinces and the employers' organizations and trade unions.
When I addressed the committee last year I took the opportunity to point out the extent to which labour representatives were serving on various boards and committees of my department and to record my appreciation of the very fine contribution which labour

is making in this way. This year I wish to repeat my words of appreciation, and it will interest the committee to know that to-day labour has 352 representatives serving on 125 boards and committees of the Department of Labour, including the Unemployment Insurance Commission. This does not, of course, give the whole picture, for labour representatives are serving on many other government bodies. It does, however, suggest a segment of the contribution which labour is making to assist the government.
The contribution of employers and other citizens in regard to these boards and committees is equally great and deeply appreciated. The manner in which men and women from all walks of life have given voluntary service in this way is one of the outstanding features of the work of the Labour department.
Current situation and future problems. In conclusion I should like to say something of the labour supply situation at the moment and suggest some of the problems which we expect to face in the coming months.
Our man-pwer statistics show that the peak of labour demand for 1943 occurred early in September with 219,000 needed. The labour requirements of A and B priority industries alone (that is of war industries and essential civilian industries) were in excess of 160,000.
During the latter part of 1943 the situation improved considerably from the viewpoint of demand, due partly, of course, to seasonal factors, but also to two causes, namely, a levelling off process in war production, and the fact that our placement plans had shown definite results.
In December, 1943, gainfully employed persons numbered an all time high of 4,288,000.
There are still some pockets of labour demand. At March 30 last, labour demand for all industries (not including logging) totalled 92,300, while there were 35,000 applicants for employment who, on that date, had not been referred to jobs.
It is difficult to predict with any degree of certainty the developments which will occur in the labour market situation during the next few months. However, it is possible to make some general observations.
It may be that further cut-backs in war production will result in other lay-offs over the next few months; thus small pockets of temporary unemployment may develop from time to time. However, it should be possible to place most of these men with little delay. There will still be numerous shortages in certain high priority industries.

War Appropriation-Labour
It is possible that some materials hitherto reserved for war production will be released for the manufacture of essential consumers' goods and so the consequent expansion in civilian production should absorb many workers of both sexes.
Men who were given military deferments because of the essential nature of their work may be made available for military service.
To sum up:
The major task of the selective service system over the next few months will be:
First, to provide the required men for the armed services; second, to meet the labour needs of agriculture; third, to place in employment men discharged from the armed forces; fourth, to meet, as they develop, the urgent needs of certain key industries; fifth, to place men laid off as a result of changes in munition production schedules as quickly and efficiently as possible.
Over the next year it appears that the general shortage of manpower will continue, yet there will be in certain localities at certain periods areas of local, though temporary, unemployment. This is inevitable in a changing war economy.
I am confident, Mr. Chairman, that whatever problems are forthcoming, my department is equipped to meet them efficient^.
I should like before I take my seat to express my appreciation of the cooperation which the Department of Labour has received in the past year. Organized.labour, employers, the provinces, particularly the departments of agriculture, the mobilization board, the various advisory boards, all have been of great assistance.
The very large staff of the department has worked hard and faithfully under considerable pressure.

Mr. Chairman, as I rise to address the committee I would crave through you the indulgence of hon. members in that I have been back in Canada but a very short time on temporary duty and have been fully occupied; I am to return almost immediately to my duties overseas. Accordingly, I have had and will have little opportunity to be in the chamber, and thus the remarks which I purpose to address to the committee may not be exactly under the item which is at present before the committee. I crave indulgence if I seem to stray to some extent from what otherwise would be in order.
It is a matter of years since I have had the privilege of speaking in this chamber, and during the last fifteen months of those years it has been my rare and distinct privilege to have been overseas on duty in the United Kingdom. Therefore my view of the deliberations of this house has perforce been a long-range view and my knowledge of its proceedings vicarious. On the other hand, the experience which has been mine as a serving officer both in Canada and overseas since the early beginning of this war has been nothing short of priceless, and I have been able to observe at first hand what has been accomplished in the service to which I am so proud to be attached, the Royal Canadian Air Force.
As I have said, I am in Canada but a short time, and it might seem a presumption on my part to take an active and direct part in the domestic deliberations of this house. Therefore in what I have to say to-day I shall speak from an overseas point of view.
Hon. members will realize as I proceed that my whole purpose in taking the time of the committee this afternoon is from a purely constructive point of view, and what I have to say is said earnestly and will, I hope, be for the benefit of the Canadian sailor, soldier, and airman. If I particularly stress the airman of that noble trio, it is because I frankly admit that I am a prejudiced witness on his behalf, a position which I know will not be misunderstood.
Those who have been in Canada in recent years and more particularly in recent months will perhaps not recognize as do those of us who have been far away from it, how much the domestic scene has changed. To return home after over a year's absence is to realize something which is, to say the least, disquieting. In the last three or four weeks I have seen, I frankly admit, only three Canadian cities, Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto, but what I have seen in those cities is to me as alarming as it is tragic. If I may generalize from these local observations I 100-155
would say that Canada at the moment is not so much a nation motivated by a full-out war effort, but is on the other hand, it would seem, in many ways a nation enjoying the greatest prosperity in its history. These days appear to me to be as gilded and as giddy as those of 1929. I regret to say it, but I say frankly that I am not particularly impressed, in the time I have been in this chamber on a few occasions, with its atmosphere. There seems to me to be an unreality about it; there seems to be a lack of appreciation in the fullest sense that the finest of Canada's young manhood is daily dying that those at home may live under British freedom. I hazard the statement that there are times when visitors may sit in these galleries for a whole sitting and then leave the house, hardly realizing there is a war on.
To have lived in a country where every- and I say "every"-able-bodied man or woman is contributing fully under an organized and well regulated selective service to what is in fact as well as in name an all-out war effort is to realize what an all-out war effort is. In the United Kingdom one does not see able-bodied men holding down jobs that could be filled as effectively by women. Those who are not in uniform are productively employed in some essential jobs, and after "working hours may be, for several nights a week, out literally all night on A.R.P. duty, fire watching, whatever it may be, back again on the job in the morning, and one or two other evenings in the week and at the weekends out at manoeuvres with the local home guard. How fully do I recognize that there are in this country tens of thousands of homes from which men have gone to duty in the armed forces, many of which homes are to-day sorrowing under the greatest tragedy that could have befallen them. But these homes are not Canada as a whole as I see it, and one cannot but feel that in the atmosphere which prevails in parts of the country which I have seen since I came back there is almost a carnival spirit, prematurely anticipating the victory which indubitably will come but which has not yet been achieved. One almost feels that the war has brought to Canada in 1944, as I have said, a period of prosperity rather than . a period of grim crisis.
During the last three or four weeks I have had the opportunity of sitting in this chamber but a few times and briefly. It has been a very sobering experience. I have not come back to Canada, as, I regret to say one who had the opportunity of meeting the enemy directly in the air or on the land or on the

M7ar Appropriation-Labour

sea. That privilege is denied me because, I am told, I am too old. My opinion of that point of view I cannot express in parliamentary language, Mr. Chairman. On the other hand, I have been in London recently and through most of England; I have returned to Canada by troopship, and therefore I have had the opportunity of seeing some activity. To see the people of England in general and the people of London in particular under the stress of the February raids on London- which incidentally were not particularly amusing-to live under the rigid rationing of the United Kingdom, to feel one's way through the blackout, is to impress upon one what might be called the grim unreality of the atmosphere of this house. Across this country from- the Atlantic to the Pacific this week, plastered on billboards, spread throughout the press, and echoed on the radio, is the slogan of the sixth victory loan, "Put Victory First". It might not be an unworthy suggestion to propose that that slogan be hung in this chamber.
I hold in my hand a copy of Hansard dated Tuesday, April 25, 1944. It records a debate about as far removed from the war as the sunny sands of Palm Beach are from the bloody sands of Anzio. I should like to ask ton. members if they would care to have that Hansard circulated among our armed forces on active duty to indicate to them what parliament is doing back home to back them up. There is the record that the proceedings of an entire day were devoted to wrangling on a motion to accept the report of a standing committee to amend the rules governing this house. I wonder what would be the effect upon the morale of those who are in the front line of this war if this debate had been broadcast to them. It was a shocking experience, particularly just at the beginning of the sixth victory loan, to have such a fatuous performance as that which was conducted in this chamber last Tuesday.
This, Mr. Chairman, is the seat of government. It is from here that stirring leadership should come. If there is a strange unreality about the conduct of this house that atmosphere will permeate the whole of Canada. On the other hand, if the government sets the pace it should, equally that atmosphere will permeate the whole of Canada. Therefore there rests that intangible and yet fully tangible responsibility on the shoulders of the government of Canada to provide that realistic, active leadership which is described in the slogan of the sixth victory loan, "Put Victory First." This is the type of leadership that this government must give. It was never more required than at this moment when we are
{Mr. Massey 1
on the threshold of the greatest and grimmest adventure in which this country has ever had
part. D-day will be news in Canada. D-day will be a stark reality to the men in the front line.
I hold in my hand three periodicals, one of them Canadian, Macleans, and two of them American, Life and Fortune. I suggest to. hon. members that they look through such publications, a.t the advertising pages. In their pages are advertisements designed to prime the public for purchases after victory. One would think, to glance through some of these pages, that victory was assured, that it was at hand to-morrow. To hear and overhear some conversations, one would be led to believe that all we have to do to win the war is to step ashore from the barges and walk to Berlin through a Germany flattened by the air force.
We must realize that no beachhead can possibly be established on the steps of the European fortress without the payment of a ghastly price. The road to Berlin can be no other than a bloody road, but that is the price we are going to have to pay before victory is ours. As I see it at the moment, Canada is all tee-ed up for a sickening shock. Some day, soon possibly, the unreality of this present era of prosperity will be brought to a sudden end by the sacrifice which this country will then realize it is making.
I do not wish to be lugubrious or morbid, but I should like this house, in its deliberations and in its plans, to think soberly upon the brave homes to which telegrams will be sent, telegrams which commence with the words, "Regret deeply...". I can say nothing more earnestly and sincerely in this chamber than I say this: In the name of every Canadian lad in the armed forces, let this house away with petty politics, away with useless and fatuous wrangling; and may this government rouse itself to the full and active responsibility of the leadership which it should give.
Never forget for a moment that this war is not won until the armistice is signed. Never forget for a moment that the fcun is not defeated, and the Jap does not cease to be a deadly menace, until the last shot is fired. Never forget for a moment that if we relax, if we take on a cock-sureness, if we assume a complacency, if we assume that victory is already ours, then the war can yet be lost.
I have said what I have said, Mr. Chairman, as strongly as I have said it, because of the impression that has been made upon me in recent days in the few times I have sat where I now stand. I say it because in some ways it is the most singularly important single thing I can say in the brief time it is my privilege to

War Appropriation-Labour
speak here. Not for a moment in anything I have said however, have I overlooked what this country has done to date. I have it very clearly in mind. I have seen at first hand the contribution it has made and is making. No more sincere compliment can be paid to the skill of the designers, the craftsmanship of the workmen, and the acumen of the business executives than is paid daily by the efficiency, the effectiveness, and the quantity on hand of the war materials which we have produced and are producing in such vast abundance. Yes, Canada's contribution in war materials is vast, magnificently effective, as our troops well know. Any Canadian who goes to the United Kingdom or elsewhere to-day may look with pride on Canada's contribution in materials to this war.
I do not profess to know directly the activities of the men in the Royal Canadian Navy or of the Canadian Army, but I know something about the men and their activities of the Royal Canadian Air Force. But for our sailors, let me say this. My station in England is adjacent to a very large naval training station, and consequently many naval officers are now numbered among my friends. Notoriously, the Royal Navy is the silent service, and any praise from a well-salt-watered naval officer is praise indeed. Repeatedly my heart has been warmed by those who have seen action in the battle of the Atlantic in particular, and in other waters in general, where they have met the Royal Canadian Navy and now speak so magnificently of its work. It was indeed a thrill a rare thrill, on the voyage home the other day to see Canadian naval vessels on duty in the Atlantic and to feel that those ships which we saw were just a few of the many of our splendid, efficient and very new Royal Canadian Navy.
Then, too, as a result of other contacts I have made, having talked to those who have sat side by side with our lads in Sicily and in Italy, and heard the words of praise that have been spoken to me sincerely, I know they are words to make any Canadian swell with pride.
Canada has every reason to be proud of her fighting troops.
And then our airmen. Groundcrew as well as aircrew, inferior to none, superior to most, have set up in this war a record which is in the best traditions, built up by that mighty group of the last war who flew their "birdcages" with gallantry and valour. The joy and the thrill of the old dog-fight have gone. Most of the sorties to-day are a pretty cold-blooded and lengthy proposition requiring the greatest courage, endurance, ability, skill and sheer guts. Youngsters of nineteen and twenty are 100-1551
captaining huge aircraft with a crew of seven and a load sometimes of eight tons of bombs, flying through flak, fighter opposition and "soup" to the target for the night, dropping their bombs with devastating precision. No nobler pages have been or are being written in the annals that record deeds of heroism, valour and courage than are being written every day and every night by the lads of the Royal Canadian Air Force.
And so I say to the government, these sailors, these soldiers and these airmen are your responsibility. They have volunteered to go. You have trained them to go. They have gone. The best is not too good for them; the least that we can do for them is the most that we can do. When I speak of the lads overseas I think too of the lads who have volunteered for overseas duty and yet who to-day are still in training stations, headquarters or other units in Canada. It is trite to say that one in uniform goes wherever he is sent and does what he is told. It is equally true. But do not criticize the volunteer in Canada who is not sent overseas. The chances are that he has repeatedly requested an overseas posting and it has not come through for him yet. I say in the minister's presence that it took me three years to get there.
Let me say a word for the ground officers and men of our air force and those airmen of our services who are denied the privilege of operations by their medical category, their age, or whatever it may be. Apparently it is altogether too easy for some to criticize those of us who are "chair-borne" and who are only permitted to fly a desk. One sometimes hears wholly unjustified and disparaging remarks about the general duties of airmen or the administrative officers. These men are just as essential to the sendees as the lads who fly. Their job may be colourless, undramatic, and in many cases routine. It is one thing to fly. It is another thing to "keep 'em flying." Aircrew is dependent upon groundcrew. We are a team; all praise and honour to the aircrew, all credit and honour to the groundcrew.
In what I have said so far I have not forgotten for a moment that this government would be most remiss in its duty, in its responsibility, if it did not plan immediately for the days of demobilization and the battle of peace, which in many ways will be just as difficult, trying and expensive as the war. It is vitally necessary that plans be made. Some plans are, of course, already in the process of making. It is vitally necessary that schemes be designed and programmes laid down now for the day when the member of the armed forces hangs up his uniform or hands it in for the last time.
War Appropriation-Labour

Let me say here that part of the functions [DOT]of my station overseas is in connection with :repatriation. Through it flew all the lads, aircrew as well as groundcrew on their way hack to Canada. I personally see and interview large numbers of them in the course of duty, and, of course, after hours. I think I can give the committee a fair idea of what is in their minds when they are at the point of coming home. I say this immediately to you: there is not one of them who wants to * be milk-fed when he comes back. There is not one of them who wants your sympathy or your pity. Goodness knows he has demonstrated to the full his unselfishness and sincerity. He has certainly proved himself a worthy citizen. He expects something from his government, and justly so. He does not want much, and he does not want to foe coddled. What he wants is reasonable, and I can tell you he expects it. All he wants from his government, to put it in a sentence, is an even break to rehabilitate himself. He realizes that he has not had too much experience in the art of living a normal life. He knows that in the last few months or years he. has lived a hectic life under a terrible strain; that inevitably that strain has taken a toll of him to a greater or lesser degree, and the period of adjustment is certainly not going to be easy for him. He wants counsel. He wants a bit of help, a bit of advice. What is already going forward in our service or in the process of development along these lines is a most worthy project, and I compliment the minister upon setting it up. Yes, the man when he returns wants help and counsel in the rehabilitation period; and yet when it comes right down to it hon. members will fully realize how little many of these youngsters, thousands of them, yes, tens of thousands of them, fresh out of school, know about earning a living or maintaining themselves. For his whole service life everything has been found for him. On the whole, the chances are he has had a pretty decent place in which to live and he has had good food. The chances are that he has earned more money than he could hope to earn in civilian life until he has had a bit of experience and has climbed up the ladder a little.
Yes, he needs your help. He certainly expects it. It would foe his idea, in which I heartily concur and -which I recommend strongly to the government, that he should be kept on strength at his rate of pay until such time as his rehabilitation period or training period for civil life, whether it foe in a school, college, university or as an apprentice in a job, or in a technical school, is complete. I do not suggest for a moment

that he feels he should be kept in uniform. He could be on leave with pay and permitted to wear civilian clothes, but kept on strength until he finishes his training.
Then he expects on his discharge, on the completion of his training, that a job be ready for him as he will be ready for it. This he feels is due him by the government. He also wants a place to live. He wants to be sure that he is going to get a place to live. There is nothing he wants more than a home. Many of these lads have been to the four corners of the world. They have been away from their country for years, and Canada looks pretty good to them when they come back. In some cases, yes, in thousands of cases, he will be bringing his bride home with him. He has already heard about the shortage of homes in Canada. He is a bit worried about that and he expects the government to do something about it.
Another thing he thinks about is the fellow who stayed back home, perhaps through no fault of his own because he was in an important war job or, maybe, because he did not want to go. The man in the services overseas appreciates fully that there is a home front as well as a war front, but he takes a pretty dim view of the fellow who could go active but did not. What he expects-[DOT] and he does expect it-is that the lad who stayed at home will not be permitted to pick off all the plums in so far as jobs are concerned before he has had a chance to get them too. In other words, he wants his future safeguarded for him while he is away. These are the principal things about demobilization which the lads I have seen are thinking about when they have time to think about their future or they find they are on their way home.
There is another point that some of them, perforce have to think about, and that is a pension. So many of them are coming back with the mark of battle upon them. Lots of them have disabilities that are permanent. W'hat about the pension? He does not like the present pension legislation. He thinks it is un-British in that the would-be pensioner is considered guilty until he is proven innocent. By that he means that the onus of proof is on the applicant. He feels it should be the other way. In other words, he feels that the applicant is entitled to his pension unless his application is proved unjustifiable. That matter is of no small importance.
He is pleased to know that his government is in the process of introducing legislation to set up three new departments, the departments of social welfare, reconstruction and veterans' affairs. He feels that is a step in

IFar Appropriation-Labour
the right direction. You see, for much of his life, just to take one point, he has had the best of medical and dental care, and his needs in those fields have been at his disposal without cost. He is going to be out on his own some day soon, he hopes; and to obtain the benefits of these necessary services is apt to be a big expense. Therefore he feels that by the time he gets back something should have been done to make these essentials accessible to him, and within his means.
Then, too, for the present, while he is still on active duty, he feels that a bit more could be done for him. About all he gets now is his pay. I am breaking no confidence, Mr. Chairman, nor am I transgressing my privileges as a serving officer or as a member of this house, when I say that I know the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) has some plans in mind in this regard, which plans it is not my privilege to mention here. To him I should like to say: All power to you and your ideas; and to his colleagues in the government I say: Give him your full support. You see, these airmen of ours are scattered over the face of the globe; some are in far-flung, distant places, remote and woolly. Sometimes some of these lads think they have been forgotten; in most cases in such places they are with a service other than their own, namely the Royal Air Force. They are still Canadians; they are still our responsibility, and they feel that their own service should look after them. So I say to the minister, carry on with the plans you have in mind; and again I urge his colleagues in the government to give him their full support in order that these plans may be implemented.
These, Mr. Chairman, are only a few of the things about which the airmen are thinking. If time permitted I could discuss other points, perhaps of less importance but still of great importance. Some of these matters have already been brought forward in this chamber by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair). For example, the clothing allowance on discharge is $65. The airman knows and the government knows, that you cannot re-kit yourself in a civvy outfit for $65; at least if you do, you look as if you had. Another thing he does not like is this quaint $44.20 for living allowance during a training period. The mathematics of it somewhat befuddles him, but he does know one thing; it is not enough. What he dislikes most of all is the vast difference between what the low-ranking airman gets on discharge as compared with what the senior officer gets. He feels that it is all out of balance and unfair. Therefore I urge upon the government, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, that they listen to what these lads of ours have to say in regal'd to
what they want and expect. Take their word for it; they have earned what they ask for. As I have said, they are not asking much; they are not unreasonable; they are not selfish; they are not grasping. This country has no finer possession than these lads. They just want a fair break; that is all. This government has no greater challenge in connection with its war responsibilities than in connection with its responsibility for the future of the men and women in Canada's armed forces.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, let me return to the point from which I began, "Put Victory First." In the midst of the planning which, is so vitally necessary for to-morrow, let this5 house never relax for a moment from its full: responsibility toward the winning of the war. Let it discourage private bickerings and! quibblings; let it set a standard for the whole of Canada, so that by its actions it may provide the leadership which this country so sorely needs. Since returning to Canada I have been asked repeatedly, "What do the lads talk about when, they are not on duty?" I can give you the answer to that question in three words: Winning the war. Visit our units in the United Kingdom, or wherever they may be; visit stations and squadrons, where our lads are in such great numbers. There you will find the noblest body of young men produced by any country. You will find their spirits high, their determination deep, never flagging or failing. To win the war; that is their slogan.
As I take my seat and then leave this chamber to return to duty I express the hope of every one of us in the armed forces, that the stern reality of the moment as we face D-day will impress itself upon this house and this countiy. Something was written during the last war which has been repeated time and time again, and it cannot be repeated too often these days. It was written by a Canadian for Canadians. They are simple words, but how deeply they should sink into the very fibre of this house and this nation: "If ye break faith ... we shall not sleep. ..."

Before the committee
takes recess I should like to place upon the record, in connection with the matter of housing particularly as it affects dependents of members of the armed forces, a telegram which was sent out by the chairman of the dependents' board of trustees to the different dependents' advisory committees all over Canada, as follows:
Immediate
Para, one: The dependents board of trustees are empowered to provide supplementary grants or special assistance to qualified dependents of members of the armed forces where such dependents have special or emergency needs.
War Appropriation-Labour

Para, two: Advisory committees are reminded that this provision covers assistance to such dependents who may be threatened with eviction and have other accommodation available but require financial assistance to meet transportation costs.
Para, three: Please arrange with your committee and your cooperating local welfare organizations to give immediate and sympathetic consideration to applications of this nature.
Para, four: Grants may be made locally as necessary within usual limits of committee authority. Where reference to the board at Ottawa is required please use telephone or telegram. Special arrangements have been made by board to deal immediately with these emergency cases.
Para, five: Your mayor and municipal authorities should be reminded immediately of the assistance available through your committee and that D.B.T. is both ready and anxious to help qualified dependents who need emergency assistance.
Para, six:	I bespeak your close personal
attention to this matter and urge the most prompt and sympathetic action. You may be assured of the fullest cooperation of the board.
Jack Pembroke,
Chairman, D.B.T.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, for a
moment or two I should like to deal with a few' of the matters to which the minister referred. I was interested in what he said about section 5, that under the present regulations it is rather difficult for an employer to discharge an employee. This change has been long overdue, and I hope it is now official that employees cannot be discharged without official consent. I am sure this will be a relief to workmen generally, particularly in large plants. I believe he said also that an employee cannot just quit his job when he feels like it. I hope the regulations referring to each of these facts, if I may call them facts, are not just something that can be set aside at will. I hope that they will be kept in force.
I wish to say a word about selective service. Tirst, I should like to compliment the minister upon his deputy, Mr. Arthur MacNamara. I have had considerable dealing with Mr. MacNamara, but it has been by correspondence and I do not think I have ever met
	, |
him. Upon the presentation of the facts to him I have always found him ready to deal with them in a proper way.
The operation of labour offices has long been a matter of inquiry with me. I have followed their operation in Great Britain and continental Europe, and I have been specially interested in the opening of labour offices in this country under national selective service. I am glad to note that national selective service are now sending its staff employees into the different plants in order that they may determine, as far as one not actually a labour operator can, just what is being done, and be in a better position to advise applicants for employment. Some time ago I talked with a young woman in the Toronto selective service office and she told me about having been sent to visit a large plant. She was quite thrilled over it,' and she said that she felt herself better qualified and more competent after that and other visits to advise those making application for various types of employment. I can see how the personnel of the selective service are acquiring an experience which will be very valuable as time goes on.
In the great plant with which I was associated for many years we had workers of many races. There were Poles, Italians, Czechoslovakians, Ukrainians, Russians and others. At all times they were found to be capable workmen. I have been wondering if the people of these races have been given a place on the staffs of selective service branches. I often think of the people who were brought into this countiy from Europe. They built up this country to a greater degree than they are given credit for. At the commencement they were brought out by the large companies for one reason or another, perhaps because of a scarcity of labour, although I can not say yes or no to that. On account of their not being able to speak English, the positions they held always entailed hard work. I am glad to see that they are now getting above that and are taking a part in other activities in this country. I should like to know if these people have been given a part in an administrative way in the operation of these offices.
I am going to suggest to the minister that he should look over the administration of his predecessor, the late Hon. Norman Rogers. I had a very high regftrd for the former Minister of Labour. He was not onb' fully qualified; he was most capable in an administrative way. He was head of the department during the deep depression, and I remember his presenting a programme to the house some time before he had the sad ending that came his way. I have often thought that

War Appropriation-Labour
had he been permitted to live, perhaps the depression would not have got down as far as it did.
The minister mentioned Steep Rock. The development there has been due largely to the ability of the hydro electric power commission to do what it did to enable the promoters of this property to divert a river which was injurious to the property and upon which was a power plant producing about
10.000	horse-power and belonging to the Minnesota Ontario Power company. The hydro electric power commission of Ontario were able to say to the owners of that power plant that if they would agree to the river being diverted they would supply them with
10.000	horse-power, the utmost capacity they were able to develop. The Ontario hydro electric power commission were able to put another dynamo into operation at their Alexander plant on the Nipigon river and provide the power.
Because of its ability to develop large blocks of power the hydro electric power commission has been of tremendous help to this country in the carrying on of the war munitions task that faces us to-day. If things should get tough for the minister after the war, I suggest that his department interest itself in assisting the provinces to produce power in a big way. I suggest to him the possibilities of producing hydro electric power in the great central province of the west, Saskatchewan. While that province produces some power from coal at Estevan and other cities, the production of hydro power, if earned' on, is only in a small way.
The minister referred to old age pensions, and I should like to say one word about this. Years ago I supported a programme which was advocated in this house by the late leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and one of his confreres, as well as a number on the then government side. This was not adopted by the government, since apparently they did not think they could get the money to carry it out. I advocated the reduction of the age limit to sixty-five years and the increasing of the contribution of the provinces, and that of the government from what is now called for by statute-S20 a month, plus what is given by the provinces, plus a war bonus-to at least a dollar a day.
The minister said something about apprentices. There, I believe, is a big field Anyone who has been associated with employment, in a big way, knows what a real system of apprenticeship in this country would do. Wp never had it. except in some of the
individual trades. I am going to suggest to the minister that between now and the next session, if this government remains in office for another year, he might prepare a programme of apprenticeship for Canada, and present it at that time. That is all I shall say about the minister's speech.
In reference to the subject of labour, itself, the minister will know that, in the years he has been acquainted with me, I have always been greatly interested in labour problems, having myself been associated with labour for many years. I have always taken the stand, and I shall never fail to take it, that the labour unions have had a much larger place in maintaining- harmony in labour ranks in Canada, and in the building up of our country, than they have been given credit for. It has been my experience that in the great majority of cases the heads of labour unions with which, when I reached the position of an executive, I had to deal were anxious to keep labour employed. I know that in more than nine cases out of ten they were anxious and willing to keep the members of their unions employed. They were not in favour of strikes. Only very rarely did a labour leader call for a strike, and then only under the greatest provocation.
Therefore I have always had a warm feeling for labour unions; and the whole labour movement from the earliest days has had a long, long struggle up, up, up, up, up, all the time, until to-day they have reached a position they never reached before. I believe it was away back in the eleventh century that what we now know as labour movements originated. They had their beginning in the early guilds, although at that time the guilds were not completely confined to labour operators, themselves, but took in various groups. Then, following the guilds came the craft unions, in the fourteenth century. In the beginning of the last century the modern labour union movement started in Great Britain, and had marvellous success. From that time on, down through the years of the last century, the work performed by great union leaders-and there have been some distinguished leaders-has been the basis of the present set-up with which the minister is so familiar, because I have no doubt that he was associated with labour unions in the old country.
I feel this way about labour unions: it was developed from guilds to crafts, and then to trade unions. Then in recent years we have found the principle of collective bargaining. I believe the former head of the labour movement in Canada, a man who commands high 'respect and who, I am pleased to know, is improving in health, must be mentioned in
War Appropriation-Labour

this connection. I believe it was in 1934 that Mr. Tom Moore-if I may speak of him lamiliarly-set out clearly and strongly the advantages of the principle of collective bargaining when he attended before the price spreads inquiry of that year. He was one of the early advocates of collective bargaining in Canada, and had to support him a bill which had been passed in the United States. Section 7A of the National Industrial Recovery Act of that country states, in part:
Employees shall 'have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representatives of their own choosing, and shall be free from the interference, restraint or coercion of employers of labour or their agents, in the designation of such representatives or in selforganization, or in other concerted activities for the purpose of collective bargaining.
From that time-and that was only ten years ago-until recently perhaps under the minister's term of office, the principle of collective bargaining has become fairly well established in this country. And I do not see why it should not be. The whole structure of plants has changed greatly in late years. Machines are automatic, and particularly those machines for the operation of which men had to be thoroughly trained. It used to take years and years of training to operate a lathe. It was one of the most complicated machines of that time. I must confess that I never could master the operation of the various gears in a lathe, so as to turn out work as it should be turned out. It was something at which I never became proficient.
To-day, however, that is largely done automatically. We find that now the single craft union in the big plant has lessened to such an extent that it really becomes necessary for the personnel of such plants, no matter what the crafts may be, to bargain together. To my mind that is the real principle of collective bargaining.
I say to the minister that the problem of employment after the war will be the responsibility of the Minister of Labour. That is in my judgment his primary duty or one of them. In the last few years, because of the operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply, and perhaps one other department, employment has got out of the minister's control. But after the war it will be his duty to look after it, and no doubt it will be back under his supervision.
I support what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey), namely, that when the troops return, those who have not positions to go to and those who will not be employed in the armies accupying a relieved Europe, or are not required in our own armed forces, or are not training in col-

leges or schools, should be kept on the armed services rolls until positions are ready for them. If that is not done, the Minister of Labour will have a terrific job on his hands.
May I express further opinions about labour. Having served for many years with many hundreds of men, I have always had a warm attachment to the labouring man and his family. It would seem that labour has suffered all the distress, and unless a big change takes place in the attitude of the state toward the labouring man, his difficulties, trials and troubles, we shall not arrive at the point at which we should like to arrive, namely the elimination of the fear of want among labour and labour troubles.
Something was said yesterday about the reduction to fourteen years of the compulsory age limit at which children should be at school. I do not agree with that. It may be all right if, as we sometimes find in Toronto, a child of fourteen years has to procure employment, and gets it upon the request of his widowed mother or perhaps the request of a father who is unable to work. In Toronto the consent of the board of education must be obtained for children to leave school at fourteen years of age. I have known cases where this has worked out satisfactorily. Of course the board requires that the child shall attend night school for so many days a week until it reaches the age of sixteen. The lad who does that will want to continue even beyond that age. I do not think the school leaving age should be less than sixteen. I agree with what was said some time ago before the reconstruction committee by a group of educationists, namely, that every Canadian child-the child of the labouring man as well as of any other citizen-is entitled to the best education that can be given it up to at least sixteen years of age. What part the minister has in this I do not know, but I believe he should insist that children be kept at school until they reach the age of sixteen. After that, what is the boy or girl to do? I have seen many cases of lads put to work for which they w-ere not equipped. I wonder whether the minister has given any thought to a suggestion which is often made here, namely, the encouragement and extension of technical schools and vestibule schools associated with industrial plants, wherein lads who are leaving school can be trained in the industry, receiving some compensation for the returns they make to the company while in training, and the foremen, seeing what progress they made, could place them in positions in the plant itself where they could get better pay than they would probably receive if they started to

War Appropriation-Labour
work without any such special training. I strongly favour giving the sons of the workers an opportunity as soon as possible so to equip themselves as to obtain the largest possible remuneration.
I also suggest that the minister interest himself in the question of whether companies, great and small, should not be permitted to use part of their excess profits, at any rate when the war is over, for the reconstruction of their plants in order that working conditions may be healthier and pleasanter. I often think with regret of men spending their lives in large dingy factories, with dark greasy walls and floors, when the companies, if they were encouraged to do so by receiving part of the excess profits which to-day must necessarily be used for the war effort, would restore and recondition their plants to the great benefit of the workers. Surely the time is coming when every plant where men and women work should be as attractive as it can possibly be made. The time is past for men and women to operate all day long under disagreeable conditions which it would not be difficult to remedy. Then, why should not every plant management do as so many plants are doing to-day, namely, give their workmen and workwomen a period of rest in the forenoon and the afternoon? I know of many plants where this rest period is in effect; indeed, if I started to name them I would take too much time, besides running the risk of omitting to mention a great many others which no doubt are doing the same thing. I therefore would simply make the general statement that many plants to-day allow their employees, as they should, as relief from the constant application which modern fast moving machines require, fifteen minutes' rest in the forenoon and a similar period in the afternoon, giving them an opportunity to refresh themselves with a cup of coffee or a sandwich. I believe that practice should be general; it does not seem fair to have it applied to a certain number of plants when it is not applied in others, although I am informed that in those plants where the practice prevails the output per employee for a similar period is greater than in factories where it has not been adopted. But the rest period should be of general application; the time has come when all workmen and workwomen, and not merely some of them, should be treated with fairness and consideration.
As I understood the minister this afternoon, he said that labour is participating to a greater extent than ever before in membership of government boards and commissions. That is as it should be. I have observed in leading history that as the franchise has been extended, so labour has taken a greater
share in the world's business. I should like to see in this house many more labour men. By this I do not mean-and I say this without making reflections upon any party or person -those who call themselves labour men; I mean those who, like the minister, have worked for years and years at the bench or with the tools of their trade, not those who serve for a couple of weeks in the summer holidays at some manual occupation and talk from then on as if they know all about labour. I am not reflecting upon any group in the house when I say that I should be glad to see more labour people in it. We all know that the government of Sweden is represented as being perhaps one of the finest governments in the world. Whether this is so or not, anyone who studied the personnel of the present Swedish parliament knows that the government contains a larger percentage of downright labour men than the government of any other country. That is a credit to Sweden.
I should also like to see in the house a larger number of business men of the type of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, men who do big things, who make big business and give large numbers of men employment. I know it is almost impossible for a man to run a business and be in the House of Commons. Nevertheless, if we had more business and labour members the work of the house would be pepped up and we should get through much earlier than we do.
What is labour entitled to? First, security against unemployment, which means, of course, security of employment. The insecurity which labour has been up against all down the years is a main reason for the stresses and troubles which have developed between employer and employee. That should not be the case. Employer and employee should cooperate, and in that regard I should like to see-and I am glad to know that the practice is spreading all the time in the plants themselves-not only the management but those under the management rising from the ranks within the factory. That is gradually increasing to the good of the factories. I have experienced that myself and I know.
I have heard people denounce industry generally, but I could show hon. members many great plants in Toronto in which all those who are managing operations, from the manager, the assistant manager, the engineers and so on right down through the plant, have been educated so to speak in the plant itself m the particular line in which they are engaged. That is as it should be. Labour cannot do it alone, nor can capital accomplish this end alone. It takes the two together,
Wat Appropriation-Labour

both capital and labour, and each has its absolute rights. The rights are not all on one side or the other.
I feel that we have reached the stage where there should be just cooperation between management and labour in every plant and just cooperation between capital and all those engaged in the plant. May I suggest to the minister that after the war his great problem will be that of providing employment. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie) has spoken of a big programme that is to be put into effect after the war to produce employment. Well, personally I do not know of any big programme. The Minister of Pensions and Natioinal Health may know of one but I do not. At any rate it is the duty of the Minister of Labour to urge, as strongly as he can, on all the departments that may be concerned the preparation of plans for employment on a large scale after the war.
We all heard the speech delivered this afternoon by the hon. member for Greenwood. It was a brilliant speech in which he excelled himself, and he pointed out that the heroes coming back after the war will want positions. He said, and I am sure we all endorse his views, that no one is more entitled to positions than those men and women who will be discharged from the services. The Minister of Labour has, therefore, a tremendous job to see to it that somebody shall make preparations for the time after the war, because the war may end sooner than anyone expects.
We have not had any difficulty in raising billions to spend on the war-for what purpose? For the destruction not only of buildings, of property, of wealth in general, but, on a large scale, of human life. I do not think as much money will be required after the war, but should it be difficult to obtain billions, if needs be, to put our men and women to work at that time? I do not think so. 1 believe that if the minister and other members of the government do their part there will be no unemployment after the war. There should be no unemployment in Canada with our incomparable resources and the thousand and one opportunities which we have to-day to do what should have been done years ago during the depression.
1 trust that the Minister of Pensions and ^National Health, who has these plans either in his pocket or in his head, will tell the house one of these odd days just where we shall send
100,000	men and women to work after the war, Decause certainly we cannot return to the condition that existed in the days of the depression.
[Mr MacNicoI.]
My time is up, and I should like to conclude by summing up these remarks as to what labour should have.
1.	Certainty of employment.
2.	Healthy working conditions. Every man and woman in Canada should have such conditions of employment.
3.	Adequate compensation to enable labour to take care of their families, and if necessary, should they have no other means of doing so, lay by something for themselves for old age. They should be freed from the necessity, if they accept the old age pension, of surrendering the right to their homes. They are not asked to do so in Australia, in New Zealand, or in England, and I do not see why they should be asked to surrender their homes in Canada if they wish to accept old age pen- . sions.
4.	There should be compensation for unemployment. We have unemployment insurance, but it is not everyone who has such insurance. No one unemployed after the war should be in a position where he will not have any revenue coming in.
5.	There should be sick benefits for the people. There have been such benefits in England for many years.
6.	I think the time has come when labour should have a larger share in plant management, assisting the managers.
7.	They should have pleasant employer-employee cooperation.
8 There should be no lock-outs. Men should not have gates locked in their faces and be sent away. The minister, I believe, has in mind setting up some board that will ensure the elimination of such a condition.
9. If there are excess profits the men should have a part of them.
Finally, I hope the government will set up a real labour board. There are now fine men in the government service who are well trained and one of whom I have in mind. He writes a great deal in the labour press. I refer to Bernard Rose, K.C., of Montreal. There are many others like him qualified to sit on such a board, and the activities of such a board would in my opinion tend to eliminate the possibility of strikes.
Surely there should be governmental machinery to keep men working and to see that they get fair play and are not chased out of employment and locked out, suffering in consequence. The time has gone by when such a condition should exist. The time has come when labour should have fair play all along the line.

May I intervene in the debate for one minute.
I agree entirely with my good friend the hon. member for Davenport as to the nature of the address heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Greenwood. It was in every way a highly effective speech, but there was one part of it in which I crave permission to make a correction, because I am sure the hon. gentleman himself would be the first to assist me in doing so. He was speaking of our comrades overseas and he said that he does not like the present pension system. He thinks it is un-British in that the would-be pensioner is considered guilty until he is proved innocent, and by that he says he means that the onus of proof is on the applicant.
It is my duty, in a cooperative spirit, to correct that statement because it might be disturbing to those overseas and to their families as well if it went out in that form. The practice at the present time is this. _ On the first hearing the responsibility is definitely on the commission to show why an award of pension should not follow, and on the second hearing, in which of course the applicant can submit additional evidence to overcome obstacles that may occur, both at that hearing and before the appeal board, there is a duty and responsibility upon the commission to set out the reasons why pension is refused.
I will conclude by quoting, not the opinion of anyone, but what is the statute law of Canada. I do so because I do not think the statement which I have quoted should go out unchallenged. Section 62 of the Pension Act reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean' that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall be entitled to draw and shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences in favour of the applicant.
This is statutory and mandatory. The hon. gentleman inadvertently used the term "unBritish". May I say to him in a kindly manner that our Canadian pension provisions are far superior to those that have been in existence in the old country, my native land, in the last twenty-five years.

My next reference is to the wage control order 9384, which was later amended by order 1727. The latter order removed some of the objectionable features of the original order 93S4, but certain aspects still remained. The cost of living bonus was incorporated into the basic rates. I would not quarrel with that if the cost of living bonus were uniform, but it is not. The result is that many of the injustices which existed under the bonus an-angement were perpetuated when the bonus was absorbed into the basic rates. In many industries the basic rates were thrown completely out of line. I do not intend to argue that too long, because anyone who wants to get in touch with those who administer wage agreements will be able to find out for himself.
Under the wage order as it stands to-day the Department of Labour, through the war labour board, has set up more or less of a dictatorship in the matter of wages. However, I think there will be one beneficial result of this; it will force the unions to go into the

question of national wage scales. By this order in council the government have attempted to regulate wages nationally, and they have practically fixed a minimum of thirty-five cents an hour. Restrictive measures are set out with regard to increases in wages. In order to get an increase you must prove that the rates are grossly unfair, but there is a little latitude if the rates are below thirty-five cents an hour. To me that means that a floor of thirty-five cents an hour is being placed under wages.
I think it is foolish for representatives of the workers to attempt to determine wage rates on a local or regional scale. I know what the mine workers are thinking about. They have been organized for a long time, and they are thinking in terms of national wage rates and of using their organization across Canada, in British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Alberta. They are thinking in terms of a national conference and the fixing of a national and uniform wage scale for that industry. That is one thing this wage control order is precipitating in the interests of the workers of this country. I believe they will grasp the opportunity and attempt to lay down national minimums in the industries over which they have jurisdiction. Perhaps in years to come those who wrote that order for other purposes will realize that they were the force that organized the workers of this country 100 per cent in their industries and established national wage rates.
In the application of the order we must realize that those who administer it are to some extent tied in with the Department of Finance, because they cannot do the things with respect to increasing wages that they would like to do, without consultation with the wartime prices and trade board. That is something which is not generally understood, because the basic principle upon which the wage controls are set is the maintenance of the price ceiling, and the avoidance of inflation. I say this is definitely working a hardship, in that certain controls are there.
We will take as an example what is classified as a non-essential industry. I have an example before me. The salt miners at Malagash, Nova Scotia, made application to the national war labour board for adjustment in their basic rates, and their application was granted. I have the finding before me, but I shall not take time to read it. This is not a large industry; it employs probably 250 or 300 people. Nevertheless it is an industry in a province which has all too little industry. The operator claims he is not able to pay the award granted by the board, unless he is permitted
to increase the price of the commodity he sells. He has made application to the wartime prices and trade board for that permission, and he is refused. He is told quite frankly that he must operate in competition with those who are importing salt into that province. Thai is competition which cannot be met. As a result of an award by the war labour board to a small industry, an industry which is necessary but which is not able to compete with importers-and they are probably subsidized, so far as I know, in the same way as applies in connection with coal-that industry is likely to close. They also have another handicap in that they have to maintain a railway line of their own in order to get the salt out to the main line of the Canadian National Railways. No subsidy is granted by the government for the maintenance of that short line, but the Canadian National, which picks up the salt at a given point, is receiving a substantial subsidy for the handling of that commodity. The picture is badly tangled up, and I am bringing it to the minister's attention. The application has already gone through all the machinery provided by his department, and I ask that he use his influence with the wartime prices and trade board to break the deadlock which exists in an essential industry.
There is no such thing as a non-essential industry. These are essential industries in the peace-time set-up, if we are to have employment in this country. It is silly to classify our peace-time industries as nonessential. Those which are now described as essential industries will cease to exist when the war is over. The other industries are essential in the post-war, and the one to which I have referred is likely to go out of existence, because of the interlocking jurisdiction which arises in connection with relieving a situation which the war labour board has already said can and should be corrected.
The wage question is a difficult one, and I am not going to labour it to-night, because I have not time to do so. The minister knows it very well, and he knows it leaves much to be desired. There are people who believe that family allowances are a solution for the inadequate wage scale. I want emphatically to state that I do not believe that. Under no circumstances must family allowances be used for that purpose.

The second point about which I would speak is that of selective service. Selective service is an organization which in my opinion requires some jacking up. At the head of it, in the minister's department, he has some of the most capable men in the country, and they are doing a very good job with, in my view, some inadequate machinery at the bottom.
The part of selective service in which I am interested to-night affects those who have the first approach to the employee seeking employment. I refer to those who give the initial interview. A boy returns from overseas, or a worker from an industry from which he has been transferred approaches selective service.
I know that mostly the approach is made in an antagonistic frame of mind. They have the feeling that they are being pushed around. The person whom they first meet, with whom they have the initial interview, is one of the most important factors in the whole set-up. His job is not a clerk's job, not one which can be handled by someone you can pick off the street because he can write down a name or read a form. Those who give this first interview should be carefully trained; they should be of the type you have on your army indue- ' tion boards, people with some knowledge of human nature, people who can question an applicant and get some idea of his aptitude for a particular line of employment. Selective service is. in fact, something to sell; the customer is the person who is seeking employment; the person who interviews him is just as important as the person you send on the road to sell a commodity for you. He must have some knowledge of the job he is doing.
Things are not working out that way now. Most of the complaints and criticisms I get in discussing the matter with those who have a grievance against selective service arise from the feeling that they are not being treated courteously; that the tendency is to get rid of them as fast as possible or to push them off to something for which they are not suited. The tendency has been to take the ablest men and put them in top positions as administrators, with the idea that these subordinate positions are just clerks' jobs which anybody can handle. The idea is wholly -wrong; it is here that you need personnel who can sell the service to a customer who is wanting to buy something.

One such case, which I think is known to the deputy minister, is that of an employee at the Ford plant at Windsor. His family was uprooted, and he is still separated from them, his wife and children being in Nova Scotia while he is at Windsor. Over a period of months I have tried to obtain payment for him for that uprooting. I met this man and took the matter up with the department at Ottawa. They immediately started action, but they have to check with the authorities in Alberta, in Nova Scotia, and in Windsor, and they are still checking.
