him not only as a friend of labour but a friend of anyone in need, that takes away much of the sadness that we feel in our loss.
I go back farther than the hon. member for Davenport in getting to the foundation on which labour is built. He went back to the eleventh century, but I go back long before that time to the day when Adam, the first man, thought he could get a thrill out of breaking the law as his wife did, and the penalty was imposed upon him in the words, "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread." From that day to the present time the individual or the nation that fails to honour that law must pay for it. As you look back you can see Macedonia falling a victim to the dishonour of the worker. Greece caught that spirit from Macedonia and they, too, failed, placing great honour in citizenship and dishonour upon the toiler. Rome caught the same spirit and, too, declined. We in this country are reminded by a distinguished man from the city of Toronto, from which some fine things come, that the country is not ruled by money but by labour. We know how true that is or how true it ought to be.
We to-day honour labour as it was never honoured before. As some of you take your minds back to the time when that very fine lady laid the corner-stone of the supreme court building, you will recall that she did not just lay that stone and then walk away. She invited the man on the scaffolding to come down as he was dressed in his overalls, and I am sure she gave him a smile that he would never forget. Thereby our present Queen Elizabeth honoured labour.
Let me go back a little bit in the history of the Department of Labour. The first deputy minister of labour is at present in the city of London, England, and he will be there to help to direct affairs so that the man who toils or the man who is the friend of the toiler shall get a square deal. The Department of Labour was first organized in 1900 under the direction of the grandfather of the Postmaster General. The first deputy minister was our present Prime Minister, and the first Minister of Labour was the same man. I would like as briefly as I can to give the committee a few of the performances of that Minister of Labour. Between 1896 and 1911 there were many outstanding acts of parliament passed in the interest of the man who toils. There was the Conciliation Act establishing the department and providing for conciliation by officers of the Department of Labour. There were the Industrial Disputes Act, the Railway Labour Disputes Act, the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, the Alien Labour Act, and on July 13, 1906, there was the
[Mr. Mclvor.l
Lord's Day Act, which gave a man the right to rest from his labours on the Sabbath, ensuring to him the right to one day in seven. That was one of the greatest boons to labour. Then there was the Fair Wage Act in 1900.
I can remember very well that in 1922 there was the amalgamation of the Grand Trunk Railway with the Canadian National Railways. The Grand Trunk railway workers were deprived of pension and seniority following the strike of trainmen in 1910 and this was restored by the Prime Minister in 1922. Then there was the act dealing with the Winnipeg post office workers. I must admit I had a hand in that because I felt they were wronged, while I did not come out very strongly in the open because I was timid. The Winnipeg postal employees were required, after the strike of 1919, to accept the minimum rates of wages for new men guaranteed rates payable for work done by statute in 1929. This was amended and they got pay and seniority as usual.
In 1917 the Immigration Act was passed whereby the minister was empowered to deport any person deemed to be advocating violence or sedition except those who were British subjects by reason of birth in Canada or naturalization in this country. This was repealed in 1929 and the section made to apply to those who are not Canadian citizens. This to me was a generous act. Then in 1922 an act was passed restricting Chinese immigration and the members from British Columbia, I suppose, would wish that the Japanese had been restricted in the same way.
Labour was given representation in 1922 upon the board of the Canadian National Railways, and Tom Moore, a man we respect very much, was appointed a member of the board. The order issued by Mr. D. B. Hanna in 1920 prohibiting employees of the Canadian National Railways from standing as political candidates was withdrawn by Sir Henry Thornton in 1922.
In 1922 we had the Dominion Government Policemen's and Firemen's Act and in 1922 we had the Public Service Retirement Act. We had the Government Employees' Compensation Act in 1925. In 1924 a committee of the House of Commons was appointed to consider the subject of industrial and international relations. The suggestion was supported by the late member for Winnipeg North Centre. There was another act in which I was interested and which in my opinion has done good work for the protection of the worker. I refer to the act concerning union labels. Wherever you see a union label you know that the piece of work on

War Appropriation-Labour
which it is found is good, honest work. That protects the working man and helps to keep him in his job.
The fair wage policy was adopted in 1900. Government departments are required to furnish monthly to the Department of Labour reports giving information as to contracts entered into during the preceding month. This is under the fair wage policy adopted in 1900. Then there was the Technical Education Act in 1919. Following representations made by labour bodies to the government in 1936, the legislation was repealed whereby unlawful associations were declared against civil liberty and against the birthright of the people. I can remember standing in this house and making my first speech against section 98 of	the criminal	code. I	do	notknow whether	I had much	influence	or	not,but I was on	the side of right and	we	wonout. Then in	1908 we had	the Government
Annuities Act, and we had the Home Improvement Act in 1937. Now we are coming close to home. In 1939 the criminal code was amended, and you can visualize standing over yonder the late Minister of Justice, the Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe; he was the one who *fathered the amendment to the criminal code which makes it a criminal offence for an employer to dismiss or to refuse to employ a worker for the sole reason that he is a member of a trade union. I have had experience, and experience does count. I remember an occasion in the city of Fort William when a man was dismissed for union activities. Perhaps he made some mistakes, but he was reinstated, and the man who dismissed him moved on.
The Unemployment Insurance Act of 1940 will stand out as a monument to the former Minister of Labour. We have many war regulations, but it wall be admitted that the outstanding piece of labour legislation that has been passed by any government in Canada is the war legislation called the labour code. It wall be remembered that when an order in council was brought in restricting wages, hon. members from all sides of the house, Liberals and those who are not, opposed that restriction and the code was amended. The seven amendments that were made to the wages control order are beautiful reading to me.
Then we have labour management. That is something to which we all agree. We agree that there should be cooperation between labour and management. It is only fair, because not all the brains of industry are confined to the office and managing staff. The man who toils has practical common sense and can see the thing to be done far better than the man in the office.
We pass on and think of the fact that during the past year men were granted holidays with pay. During the past year 600,000 men received holidays with pay. This is a great boon to the man who toils and it is to the credit of the first deputy minister of labour. Then we have labour representation on the wages control board, the cost of living bonus, and so on. When a man wishes to go from one job to another, if he asks the superintendent of selective service for permission, he is protected. He does not lose his job, neither does he lose his unemployment insurance card. He can be reinstated. I shall not take up the time of the committee to speak of the health and recreation facilities that were made available, the care that was taken of the toiler in the war production plants. I could speak of the comfort that mothers who have to work get from the assurance that their children are well taken care of.
I have a question to ask the Minister of Labour, and I should like him to consider it very closely. I do not think it is in the labour code. Should not those who work on a job, no matter what kind of job, be paid equally? There are some jobs that a man can do better than a woman. There are some jobs that a woman can do better than a man. I think a man would make a better policeman or fireman than would a woman, but a woman makes a better nurse. I have found that when male nurses' were employed they were paid better than the women. There are jobs and w'ork that are suitable to each. If the same work is done by a man or a woman they should have the same pay. That is only fair. If a woman does the same work as a man is doing, who gets the advantage if the pay is not equal? It is certainly not the man; neither is it the woman; it is the employer. I suggest to the Minister of Labour that the same pay be given for the same work, no matter whether it is done by a man or a woman.
Labour in Canada has its difficulties. The labouring people are just like lawyers. They may quarrel among themselves, but when they have a common cause then they can work together. You have seen lawyers fight like everything in a court and then go out and enjoy refreshments together. I think that is very much like labour to-day. When they have a common cause they will forget their differences and fight their common enemies. When I think of the growth of labour in Canada I am extremely proud of being associated with them. I have had a lot to do with them. I think the man who toils to-day is a credit to Canada. Labour has done an outstanding job in war production.
War Appropriation-Labour

But the problem will arise after the war. We have some prophets who tell us there will be great unemployment after the war. I do not believe a word of it. With our present Minister of Labour and Minister of Munitions and Supply I do not think that will ever come. Of course, if others take their places I may not be so confident. But every man should have a job and every effort should be made to see that he gets one. I hope I shall never see the occasion arise when the men have to ride the rods again. If they ride the rods I will ride with them, because we have enough in this country to satisfy the needs of everybody here and a great many more if we can get them to come here.
I pay my tribute to the Department of Labour because I go in and out among its officers. I find a great many of them, are saturated with the desire to help the men who toil, and most of them have in their vest pocket a union card.

It is not often that I have to follow in a church a pulpit orator like the hon. member who has preceded me. I may say if I were a pulpit orator I hope that I would draw a better audience than we have here to-night, because once upon a time I have drawn audiences of three, four and five thousand people.
We have on the government benches to-night eleven on one side, and five on this side. We have here about me eleven or twelve Conservatives and there are five members of the C.C.F. party, two of the Social Credit party and one who' is Acting Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada. The members are tired of long debates. I am sure the hon. member who is acting as Attorney General, sitting in the seat of the learned hon. Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada will do a great deal to set things right.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: This is the first Friday night that the hon. member has been here.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
It is not. I have been here the last three Friday nights. I am not in the habit of addressing audiences of this size. I wish to say to the Department of Labour that I have been a consistent supporter of labour all my life. During my long public career, which I started in 1905 as an alderman in the city of Toronto, I have always had and maintained the consistent support of the overwhelming majority of the labour people of the city from which I come. Along with my late leader in the province we fought for the public ownership of light, power and transportation, and we enjoyed the support of a large part of the labour of that province
[Mr. Mclvor.l
which was. engaged in that fight. The attainment of that objective brought joy to the cities and towns of Ontario and to the industrial workers and farmers. Cheap electrical power and light were made available to nearly all the farms.
I have never been one of those who thought they know something about this problem; far from it. I look upon the House of Commons as a sort of gentlemen's club where everybody has divergent views. As long as they express them sincerely and clearly I have no quarrel with them; far from it. I always listen to hon. members with a great deal of respect.
I have no quarrel with the Department of Labour, which the present minister took over at a critical time. If only we had had organized national selective service at the beginning of the war we would have been far better off; but unfortunately we did not; we did not adopt the policy that was followed in the mother country, where they were just a few minutes away from the bases for the planes which carried the bombs that nearly engulfed civilization. The mother country went it alone for two years, and with the aid of the glorious young men whe flew her planes she saved civilization. The working class and all other classes in Britain rallied to the colours and saved the world.
I repeat, it was most unfortunate that we did not have national selective service from the beginning, because the people of Canada were simply looking for leadership which they were not given. The country was not prepared for war, and perhaps the government were not prepared to go the distance they should have gone. In my view the entire situation was handled very badly for the first two years of the war. I never quarrel with the officials of a government department, because, after all is said and done, the backbone of any government, whether federal, provincial or municipal, is the permanent officials who advise the heads of departments, and we have a most able body of officials, who are loyal, sincere public servants of Canada and a credit to this country.
I have some respectful criticism to offer, but first may I say to the learned hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who is one of our best pulpit orators, that it is not usual for one orator to talk to another pulpit orator, especially when it is the Church that is speaking. I have great respect for hon. gentlemen down in the corner; they are becoming the pride of the haberdashers, but perhaps some of the things I have to say will be of interest to thc-m. I do not like to see returned soldiers in the city from which I come going about trying to find someone to advise them

War Appropriation-Labour
as to what they should do. One or two of the newspapers have been criticizing that situation. I have had a great dead of confidence in the present deputy minister of labour since he cleaned up the dependency situation; I have often praised what he did in that connection in 1940, during the darkest hours of the battle of Britain. He comes from Winnipeg. he admits that, but it should not be held against him. I wish to point out to the minister, as I pointed out to his predecessor, that if I were a soldier coming coming home I would rather go and see a clergyman than go to some of these government offices. To-day I believe the average clergyman is doing a great deal of social work; I know the clergy of the diocese of Toronto, and that is so as far as they are concerned. When our soldiers go to the selective service offices trying to get jobs, the clerks have not time to interview them; they are sent home and told to come back the next day. I would far rather go to the office of a clergyman, because he could tell me where to go; probably he would know some of the aldermen or some members of parliament. In fact, some clergymen are great admirers of the Minister of Pensions and National Health, the master of ceremonies of the house. I sometimes think of him as the Beau Brummel of the cabinet, but around eleven o'clock at night he becomes the master of ceremonies and tells us in a most genial manner what we are to do the next day.
I want to point out to the government in all seriousness that it is not fair to expect returned men to travel all over the city looking for employment; many times they have to walk because they have no car tickets. There should be some solution to this difficulty. If national selective service cannot handle them, turn the job over to the municipalities so that these men may be looked after. Why should a poor soldier just off the train have to come home to his wife and family and say, "Well, I was down town and called at two or three departments, but they told me to come back again tomorrow." I hope that situation will be remedied. There should be no necessity for these men to keep going back; some other system should be introduced. After the last war there was a great deal of trouble in this connection, and unless we bestir ourselves I am afraid we shall have the same trouble after this war. We have heard a good deal about reconstruction. I would remind the minister that even now some industries in the United States are being converted to peace-time work. I am not altogether satisfied with our stay-at-home army of sixty or seventy-five or one
hundred thousand men; we have had various estimates as to the size of it. If these men are required only for home defence many of them should be returned to industry, because in my opinion there is no such thing as home defence. Wars are won by soldiers, sailors and airmen at the scene of combat; that is where they are useful. I know many men who have been called up and sent all the way across the country, at vast cost to the government. Every train is crowded with men, some of them travelling from Vancouver to Halifax. That is a nice ride, I must admit. I have made that journey only twice; I have no time for rides. We waited until the third year of the war before bringing in national selective service, but now a great deal of money is being wasted. According to government reports, in 1941 the Canadian National received $2,500,000 and the Canadian Pacific was paid $2,750,000. It is just a waste of money transferring men from work with which they are familiar to work they know nothing about, and during the coming year I believe this matter should be looked into.
As I said, some industries in the United States have begun the conversion to peacetime production. They are not slackening their war effort, but they find that in some products they are overstocked and that the demand has ceased for others. In Washington the other day they wanted to get two million electric toasters, but they did not know to whom they should give the order, since the production of toasters has been curtailed for the last year or two. Finally they decided to place the order on the quota system. So far I have not heard of anything being done in Canada to convert our industry from a war-time to a peace-time economy. We must not forget that it has been a basic principle of economy ever since the early Roman days that after a great war each countiy must look after its own people first. After that is done they can begin to talk about international affairs. We have a committee on reconstruction, but they are building too many castles in the air. At the present time we have facing us a list of bills which will keep us here until Christmas; we shall not be out of these trenches until_ then. Before we get through here we shall be going down to Sparks street to buy a few Christmas presents, though no doubt the government will not be able to get through many of the bills which are proposed. A lot of them are only castles in the air. When we are talking about social security and reconstruction we must not forget that after the war this country is going to be desperatejy poor.
War Appropriation-Labour

We have squandered our national resources at an awful pace and the result is that the people of this country will have a tremendous debt to pay. The state has no money for all these things. Where is the state to get the money? One would think they were able to mine tons of gold from the north country to pay for all these items of reconstruction and nostrums that are being proposed. I have been a Christian socialist all my life, and I supported the people in Ontario who advocated these measures long before the C.C.F.
When the war is over we shall have to go back to the old way of life. They are getting back to it in England. They have what they call the trade war practices act which is putting industry, large and small, back to where it was without all these controls, back to where it was before the war. Wholesale and retail business are beginning to get together. People seem to think the state is going to pay for all these things, but the fact is that generations yet unborn will have to help to pay for them. I believe in the principle of private enterprise. It has not failed, although it has made some mistakes and will, no doubt, have to clean house. It is doing as much as it can in the way of paying for these things. If we gave private enterprise a chance it would be our best source of employment after the war and do more to reestablish things than anything else.
They had a meeting a short time ago in the city hall at Edinburgh, Scotland, with thirteen speakers in the morning and fourteen in the afternoon. That is a total of twenty-seven, much better than we are doing here. They talked about reconstruction, and the statement was made that the home is gone. Some of the socialists claimed that the state would have to take the place of the home. The moderator of the Presbyterian church spoke at that meeting. I have heard two or three moderators once in a while because I am a moderate myself. The moderator told them about delinquency and all that kind of thing which was caused by the young people not having work to do. He told them that necessity was the mother of invention and that the homes should be reestablished. I think he was quite right in what he said.
In the early, days this country was settled mainly by people from the British isles. The English and French got along well together because, as a rule, they were poor people. They hewed down the forests of Ontario, Quebec and other parts of this country. They did not have any of the things that are proposed to-day to be done by the state. The state cannot do anything unless it is paid
[Mr. Church J
for by the taxpayers. Are you going to raise the income tax? Are you going to put more taxation on the business man? The minister should look into the coal situation and the national fuel supply which was brought up by the Conservatives in 1921.
There is also the question of housing. We have been told that this is not an emergency. Then there are the questions of food and civil aviation. Russia will require generators and other electrical goods after the war. Our shipbuilding plants will have to be kept going. There are many other things that will have to be done. The reconstruction committee has done a lot of hard work, and I know the members of that committee have given a great deal of time and attention to their task.
I referred the other day to the Atlantic charter. Before this reconstruction can go on any further we shall have to decide some things first. We shall have to decide what we are going to do about the imperial preference, about favoured nation treaties and things like that. The Atlantic charter provides expressly for imperial preference. We shall have to decide about lower tariffs. In my opinion there will always be tariffs. It is all very well to talk about things, but we should wait until we see what happens at the peace table. Why should we throw away our best customer, the mother country, for others when we do not know what they will buy? The mother country has always been our best customer for grain and many other things. I believe we should stick to the empire which is our best customer.
Reference has been made to certain other matters, one of which is national selective service. I do not think we are getting the results we should for the money we are spending. The vote last year was $9,800,000, whereas this year it is $11,000,000. We should get some results for this money. When one looks over the list of men I think some of them might just as well be back in trade and commerce and industry and agriculture instead of our spending all this money upon them. They should be ready to return to industry unless they are prepared to fight the battles of this country at the front.
The minister, his deputy and others have been attending a convention. I have no objection to this, since I think they deserve a holiday because of the way they have worked. However, I do not think we should be considering international socialism when we do not know who is going to win the war. This convention at Philadelphia is part of the old League of Nations, now defunct. I support the international labour convention. This house has never voted any money for it. I

War Appropriation-Labour
never was a believer in the League of Nations because I think it was one of the things that caused this war. I cannot see just what good that meeting at Philadelphia will do because we do not know where we stand. Until the war is won, the war is primary. I am in favour of having conferences with the empire first of all. I think these international labour bodies will have a mission in the world to come. We hope it will be a better world for the working classes.
Something has been said about the Conservative party. The Progressive Conservative party was the pioneer, in both federal and provincial fields, with nearly all the social legislation we have in this country. They were the first to advocate the public ownership of our light, power and transportation facilities. They set up a national system of railways and they have advocated the development of water power for the benefit of the Canadian people. Ontario gave the public the workmen's compensation act, and many other statutes. It was the Conservative party in this house which in 1921 proposed a national system of unemployment insurance, prison reform, health insurance, and other social measures such as old age pensions and a national fuel policy. I had resolutions with respect to those things myself, in 1921, when I was first elected to the house.
It cannot be denied that in Canada and in England Conservative members of the House of Commons have worked for all these institutions. It cannot be denied that the Progressive Conservative party in this country and the Conservative party in the old country have produced a long line of great statesmen who have known how to tread the middle path of ordered progress and to sow a political harvest which subsequent generations of our empire have reaped a thousandfold. After every war we have brought about reconstruction and all that kind of thing.
It was Clarendon who restored Church and King on the basis of those admirable and incomparable laws of government; Danby who founded the party system; Edward Seymour who, by sponsoring the Act of Settlement, paved the way for the Protestant succession; Harley whose practice led to the adoption of the principle that the crown acts through responsible ministers; William Pitt the younger who revived the idea of the strength of parliamentary government when compared with the rule of the terrorist mob, and who gave the world and his country a priceless legacy of British opposition to arbitrary government and dictatorship; Peel who brought free trade to his country and converted the middle classes to Conservatism; Shaftesbury who stirred the
conscience of his party on the urgent need for social reform; Disraeli who linked imperialism with democracy and issued his resounding appeal for the "two nations" of rich and poor to unite; Randolph Churchill, who in a brief life of intense activity gave colour and direction to the policy of conservative democracy; Joseph Chamberlain who fought for imperial trusteeship and brought idealism into imperialistic economics; Baldwin and Neville Chamberlain whose financial "revolution" gave new life to British industry in the thirties and unconsciously paved the way in no small measure for the mighty war effort of the forties; Winston Churchill who led the country in its finest hour. Those are some of the men. And I can tell you this, that the ranks over there in the mother country are filled with young Conservatives who can take their places.
So far as this particular bill-of-fare of the minister is concerned, there is a great deal of good in it. I agree with much of what was said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I agree with what he has said about education. A great mistake has been made there. I began public life by serving on a school board, and I know something about the low salaries of public school teachers. The mistake made at the time of confederation was that education was not made concurrent. There should have been concurrent jurisdiction, because it is the duty of the government to look after the health, peace, prosperity and success of its people, and especially of the rising generation. The government did give a lead with respect to technical education. I am surprised to hear the hon. member say that in his municipality salaries have been as low as $150. I believe in Toronto our high school teachers are paid as much as $4,000.
I am glad to see that the minister is providing some money for universities, in connection with medicine and dentistry. I hope there may be some amendment. Probably the minister is going a little too far when he asks these students to get fifty per cent of their marks on their examination, on penalty of not being allowed to continue. There will be a great scarcity of doctors. And, by the way, I see a very fine doctor sitting over here, a university man, who graduated from the medical school of the university of Toronto. I can remember the hon. member's name, but I do not remember his seat. Sometimes I remember the seat, and do not remember the name. The late Minister of Justice had great difficulty in remembering the name of the constituency of the hon. member for Greenwood. He could not remember that it was Greenwood, but after the speech made by
War Appropriation-Labour

the hon. member for Greenwood to-day, I am inclined to think there it not much "green" about it.
I do hope the minister will revise the provision with respect to universities, which states that only those who get fifty per cent or more of their marks can go back to school. Let us not forget that some of these young people have brothers at the front. These boys who are at school now are the junior members of their families, and many of them work all summer in order to get enough money to pay their school fees.
I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, with respect to low salaries. Some of those boys have to work hard to scrape up enough money to go to university. They are poor boys, from poor families, but they are most brilliant graduates. I know that the most brilliant graduates the university of Toronto has had from her school of science have had to work all summer to earn their fees. I hope something will be done to amend that regulation before it is too late.
I see my friend the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Roebuck) who was at one time attorney general of Ontario. I believe the university of Toronto is dear to his heart. He knows about this condition, and I am just pointing out to the minister that there should be some revision in the university course by allowing these boys who have to work to earn their fees to pass their examinations without too great difficulty. Some of these boys have brothers and sisters engaged in war work; the fathers of some of them are at the front, and it is my hope that some amendment will be made. We need all these young engineers, young doctors and young dentists, and I do not see how they can complete their courses in the time allowed to them. It would be my hope that there might be some meeting arranged to look into this matter. The deputy minister, who has done a great deal for the universities, did, I understand, have a meeting with university officials. I hope he will see fit to revise this legislation before next fall.
I hope something may be done along the lines of a national coal supply. There may be some other "church" members here to-night. I notice the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor)-probably he is one-is going to take another pulpit, and probably will preach twice in one evening. But I think he has departed for this evening. I have no hymn to announce to close the prayer meeting, but I do want to say that if this is the bi!l-offMr. Church.]
fare, then I do not see much in it for the average working man, when he comes home from war.
After all is said and done, the young men who come back from this war may never live normal lives again. Every day I receive letters from parents who have lost their sons. Just to-day I received half a dozen of them. These are young people who have been killed, young men of eighteen or nineteen years, who a year ago were going to high school. It is an awful thing to think about. To-day I was told about two young boys who were killed, and who had been going to McGill university in the fall of 1940 and 1941. Now they are killed. There have been about 860 from the high schools of my city alone.
I hope that when our men get back from the war we shall have something practical as a bill-of-fare to give them. I have dozens of them who come to see me every week-end. They' are very much disappointed. I cannot [DOT] tell them to whom they should go, because I do not know. We are not supposed to know where all those offices are. I hope the minister will see if this procedure cannot be simplified, with the cooperation of the provinces and the municipalities.
I had anticipated that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) would have been ready to go on to-night.

speechtext: He is here, anyway.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
But if he is not here I
will call on the hon. member for West Kootenay (Mr. Esling).
I think my time is almost up, and I notice the attorney general is looking at me. I can only say this, that while I wish to give the government independent support, I must say that a great many mistakes are being made. Of course I know a great many mistakes will be made, but I do hope the minister will hearken to some of the handwriting on the wall before it is too late. I hope he will not be taking people out of jobs for which they are fitted, and put them to work chopping down trees. What good would we be at chopping down trees, except to get some new timber for a platform. That is all I can see in this chopping down of trees, when there is no pulpwood, and even the publisher of the Chicago Tribune will have to trim this log cutting and reduce the size of his paper if we go on in this wray.
As I see it, there is no use in taking young people out of drug stores and grocery stores and sending them up to New Ontario to chop down trees. We know what we did before. I remember when the Grenadiers and the

War Appropriation-Labour
Footguards and the Queen's Own marched across lake Superior at 44 degrees below zero-men taken out of stores, clerical people and the like, under the command of Colonel Dennison: they saved this country from dis-intigration, and not one red cent have they got from that day to this. I would add a reference to the fine battalion from Lunenburg, Nova Scotia; I saw them at the foot of Jarvis street when I was only knee-high. In those days there was a large number of public houses around the city hall, at the foot of Jarvis street, which distributed sandwiches and glasses of beer to the boys; but when the soldiers came back they never received any pay; that was the sort of treatment which was given to the veterans in those days. I hope that this time and in the days to come there will be a different way of treating those who serve the country; and I am not in favour of this idea of sending this class of people out to chop down trees.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
I wish to draw to the attention of the minister a few facts about those who are labouring with the sick in this country. Of about 11.000 doctors in Canada, some 4,000 have been inducted into war service, and this has made things very difficult for the remainder who are working with the civilians. Many of these doctors are overworked and cannot possibly attend to all who require their services, and in large districts there are no doctors at all. This is a serious situation, especially with the shortage of gasoline, tires and means of transportation. The action taken by national selective service in assigning some doctors who are in uniform to these rural districts and giving them support was a move in the right direction, and it should be extended, so that there will be less suffering through lack of medical care in the far distant areas of this country.
In the nursing and hospital situation there is also a shortage of assistance. I recently read, in the book entitled, "Canadian Hospitals," of April, 1944, that although there is a long waiting list of patients desiring to enter two sanatoria, 168 beds in those two hospitals are being kept idle because of a shortage of nurses and orderlies and assistants in those hospitals. That condition applies to other hospitals in the country, and it is a serious matter, because if a tubercular patient is kept out of hospital he or she is a serious menace, because of the nature of the disease, to those who are attending that patient. More than that, surgical procedure -will often cut short the course of these diseases and hasten the recovery, and that surgical procedure can only be taken in well-equipped hospitals.
The nursing situation is, I think, particularly bad in some of the smaller hospitals. It is true that nurses who have retired, nurses who have married, who have given up their regular work, for the sake of the service have gone into hospitals ^nd done excellent work, and I would pay tribute to those nurses who have volunteered in this time of great need. It may be true that some nursing sisters are holding back to work in private practice and possibly making good fees, but as a general rule the nurses have tried to do their best. There again, however, complaint is frequently made that hospitals cannot compete with military organizations in holding these nurses. I know the minister and the deputy minister have given this matter a, good deal of attention, and I assure them it is an important problem and a great difficulty which is facing those who are managing hospitals and trying to carry on the work at the present time.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
I invite the minister to bring the committee up to date with a report on the Doukhobors. A year ago we had the benefit of the report which the mounted police had made, which was brought down, I think, in the month of March, and attention was drawn to the state of affairs revealed therein, which was, I believe, that some thirteen hundred of them had not submitted for registration. Since that time, of course, others have reached the age of sixteen years and should have registered. I do not propose to make a statement this evening on the subject of the Doukhobors. I did so last year and the previous year, and I recollect that the minister in his reply, which was but short, suggested that if the matter were left in his hands for another six months he might be able to report on what progress he had been able to make.
I should like the minister to describe the position first with regard to Saskatchewan, how the registration has gone there, to what extent have the provisions of the National Resources Mobilization Act been carried out, and, in that those Doukhobors of the proper age for military service would not be subjected to military service but would have to be used in alternate employment, to what extent he has been able to have these men do alternative service, whether it has been necessary to institute prosecutions, and to what extent those prosecutions have been carried out.
I should like the minister to deal with the matter in that way if he would be good enough to do so, because from there on the story can be taken up in British Columbia. Unfortunately it is evident that these Doukhobors have been travelling from Saskatchewan and adding to the difficulties in British

War Appropriation-Labour

Columbia. As the minister is well aware, there have been infractions of the law in British Columbia of recent times, and action has been taken to stop indecent parades and the like. To my mind, the real grievance that the people whom I represent have is that the law apparently is not being "administered equally for the Canadian citizens and for the Douk-hobors, and I shall be very much obliged if the minister will report on the situation and bring us up to date with information.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: My hon. friend mentioned Saskatchewan first. The situation there has been cleared up and the Doukhobors are complying with the law. In certain parts of Alberta the situation is not as good as it is in Saskatchewan and, as my hon. friend knows, in British Columbia the situation is difficult and always has been.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: What does the minister mean when he says that the law is being adhered to in Saskatchewan? Take those who are of such an age that they would have to go into military service but for their peculiar views. Have they gone into alternate camps?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Not necessarily camps but into alternate service. We have a diversification of alternate service. If a man is better fitted for agriculture that is where he goes.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: And they receive $25 and the rest goes to the Red Cross.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
Yes, absolutely. In
British Columbia, I am frank to admit, the situation is difficult; I would not be honest if I did not make that admission. It has been difficult for all governments since the Doukhobors came to Canada. Conferences are taking place between ourselves and the government of British Columbia in connection with the better observance of law and order among the Doukhobors in that province. The other evening I was talking to a large industrialist on the way from Montreal, and he indicated to me that the Doukhobors in this particular part of British Columbia were doing really good work at Brilliant, if I remember rightly.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: What kind of work?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: They are labourers.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: The pictures indicate that they are doing a strange kind of job.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: That might be true, too. It is very difficult. My hon. friend can rest assured that as far as humanly possible we are measuring up to the situation the best we know how, and I cannot go further.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Are prosecutions being carried) out?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Yes. Recently we have carried out prosecutions in British Columbia.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
What has been the result
of those?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: What my hon. friend referred to; that is what happened. That is the result of the prosecutions.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
Is that their sole
punishment?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: There have been some nude parades since the prosecutions.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Does the minister consider he has a sufficient police force to handle the situation?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: That is not his department.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Primarily the duty of enforcement is on the local authorities and then on the provincial authorities. We have not been requested to go and enforce the law. It is primarily the duty of the local authorities, then the provincial authorities, and if that cannot be done the federal authorities step in.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
I do not want to question the minister's word with regard to that, but I gravely doubt whether that is the correct answer. I should like the Minister of Justice to tell us what the situation is. My information is that on a recent occasion the attorney general of British Columbia had the advantage of discussing the matter with him; I understand that the police force which should be called on for this matter is the mounted police, and the mounted police should have the assistance of the provincial police if it be necessary.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: There is no duty on the mounted police, as suggested by the hon. member for Yale. The administration of the province of British Columbia in that regard is under the jurisdiction of the attorney general. There was an occasion some Weeks ago when difficulties were anticipated, and there were communications between the attorney general's officers and the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It was arranged that a detachment would be ready to move into a certain locality if they were requested to do so, but fortunately that did not become necessary.
There have been prosecutions, from what I learn from the newspapers. There have been prosecutions for indecent exposure and several persons have been convicted. We had within the last few days a communication from the warden of the penitentiary, accompanied by

War Appropriation-Labour
clippings announcing that there had been condemnations to the penitentiary of six women and some thirteen men, I think, and I am not in a position to state at this moment what has occurred since. Arrangements were made to transfer these women who had been condemned to the penitentiary to the only penitentiary for women that is maintained in Canada, and I am unable to say whether they are now on their way from British Columbia to that penitentiary or not. It was anticipated that there would have to be wardens and matrons to accompany them, and authority was given to the penitentiaries branch to make proper arrangements with a railway company to have a special car in which these prisoners, and those who would have to accompany them, would be sequestrated and might not mingle with others travelling on the same train. There had been some suggestion that they might be brought by air from British Columbia to the penitentiary for women, but after investigation it was found that this would not be practicable and the other method is the one that was authorized. But I am not at present able to say whether they have arrived or are on their way. There have been suggestions that very rigorous methods of enforcing the regulations against the whole of the Doukhobor population should be adopted. There are a great many cases, something over 18,000 reported cases throughout Canada, of failure to comply with the regulations.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
18,000?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	Something over
18,000.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
With regard to registration?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Failures of every kind to comply with the regulations under the mobilization act. There are some failures to register, failures to comply with orders to report for medical examination, failures to report to camp after medical examination has been had, and so forth. The prosecutions are usually handled by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The usual procedure is for the registrars in the district when they have a file showing non-compliance with any one of the regulations to turn it over to the R.C.M.P. for investigation and prosecution if the investigation warrants prosecution.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
That is exactly what I
suggested, and I understood the minister to say that it was not the R.C.M.P. that carried out the prosecution.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police do make investigations. When the registrars turn the files over to the 100-1561
R.C.M.P. they do deal with them, but in respect of the Doukhobor the complaint, as I understand it, is that the first step has not been taken. The registrars have no files concerning them. What would have to be done would be to go through the province and check on the possession or non-possession of a registration card by each individual.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
The fact is they have none. Very few of them have registered. I suppose that is the case.	,
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I think a large majority of them have not registered at any time. The suggestion has been made that a sufficient force should be raised to make the investigations and to compel them to register. The commissioner of the R.C.M.P. was of the opinion that there were not large numbers who' were not engaged in useful work and who would, in fact, be transferred to work other than that which they are performing at the present time, and that the number of men who would be required first of all to make the investigation and then to make the show of force that would have to be made to compel compliance would be out of proportion to the benefit that could be expected from any attempt to speed up what is being done.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
If the minister would permit me, the difficulty that remains is that the Canadian boy is proceeded against if he does not register, does not carry out the necessities of the act, and the minister calmly says now that no good would result from dealing with the Doukhobor, and yet they live side by side in those communities with Canadians. I think it is absolutely unfair to the Canadian boy.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The unfairness is not, I think, as apparent as the hon. member would suggest. I do not think there is any unfairness to anyone in having to comply with the regulations. In respect of those Doukhobors who are entitled to the benefit of the exceptional treatment provided by the orders in council under which they came to this country, may I say this? Under the terms of those orders in council they are not required to perform military services. Now quite wrongly they feel that any compliance with the mobilization act or with the statute requiring national registration would be a first step toward military service, and many of them refuse to take that step. The most that could be expected from them would be to get them into alternative service. The alternative service would probably have to be performed under conditions where their earnings would be more than the portion that they would be entitled to keep. That is the only benefit the-
24S2

War Appropriation-Labour
public would receive from the mobilization of the men required to enforce the regulation against them beyond the other feature of having everyone realize that he has to comply with the Canadian laws. That, I appreciate, is very important; but it was felt at this time that the R.C.M.P. could not afford the number of men that would be required to give special preference to the Doukhobor problem.
For several months the R.C.M.P. have had a large backlog of those files that have been coming forward in the normal way in the various registration divisions of the country. These are so numerous that they are not diminishing the outstanding number very rapidly. Some progress is being made in disposing of more cases than are coming forward from month to month, but there is still a substantial backlog. The R.C.M.P. have to deal with those because the files are turned over to them by the mobilization officers. The other feature would require quite a large corps to seek out those who have not even registered; and it has not been found possible to make that number of R.C.M.P. personnel available. When I said to the hon. member that it was not the responsibility of the R.C.M.P. to handle the Doukhobor problem, I was referring to the suppression of those disorders that have arisen in the district.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Oh, yes; that is another 4hing.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: That is being handled *by the provincial authorities, and there is this understanding: The R.C.M.P. are prepared to supply personnel from the localities where they *can be spared, if and when required to do so by the attorney general of British Columbia.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
The minister agrees, therefore, that in infractions of the regulations with regard to registration it is the R.C.M.P. who take action.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	It is the R.C.M.P.
who are called upon by the registrars under the mobilization act when they have knowledge of an infraction.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
Will the minister be good enough to say whether any of those 1,333, who were believed to be unregistered as a result of the report of the R.C.M.P., have since registered? Could he say that registrations are now going on particularly with regard to those who have become sixteen years of age and who are consequently subject to the registration since the time of this report and since the year 1940 when registration was put into force? In other words, could he tell the
(
committee how many of these people in southern British Columbia have snapped their fingers at registration and have not registered?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Some of them have registered, but I do not think a great number. I could not give the exact figures of those people who have snapped their fingers at the regulation, as my hon. friend has suggested.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: No doubt thousands of them have not registered.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Could the minister give us any information with regard to the bottleneck that has become apparent in packing plants throughout Canada consequent upon the transfer of labour from those plants to the farms? Live stock have become marketable; the yards are full and the packing plants cannot get the help to take care of them. It has been suggested that some of these men should be transferred back to the packing plants. Experienced men went back to the farms on April 1, and the bottleneck has been the consequence. Could the minister give us any information on that?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is speaking of the packing situation generally across the country? Twice as many people are engaged in the packing industry to-day as there were in 1939. In the last season we put 4,(XX) additional people into the packing industry. I should like to say this about the packing industry: it is hard work, and requires men with strong backs and strong arms. I think we generally recognize that feature of it. What we did was we made possible the transfer of men from agriculture to the packing plants and so on. Many of these men were owners of farms, and when spring came along and it was time to seed, they went back to their farms. It has been said that some of them went back because they felt the special consideration given to agricultural workers under the mobilization regulations would be withdrawn if they stayed in the packing industry. We indicated clearly, and in fact instructions were sent to our officials in the field, that these men could stay in the packing industry and enjoy the same rights, if you call them rights, that were granted to agricultural workers generally. We appreciate that there is a shortage of labour in the packing industry at this time, but constant attention is being given the problem and it is no worse now than it was three months ago. It is this rush of cattle and hogs to the packing plants that has brought about the difficulty. I should like it clearly understood, however, that to-day we have twice as many people working in the

War Appropriation-Labour
packing industry as we had in 1939, and that selective service has made possible the continuation of that industry on a much larger scale than was the case in the days of peace.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: Is it not a fact that instead of a shortage of labour in the packing plants the abattoirs and freezers are so full that they cannot handle the meat which is being processed at the present time?

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: I could not answer that question; I deal with the man-power end of it and do not know much about any other phases of the industry.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: I have had some correspondence from the west in regard to the backing up of hogs on the farms, and it is serious. When a' hog reaches a certain weight it should be marketed. The information I had from Saskatchewan was that last week the stockyards were full of hogs, and that an embargo was imposed at some of the shipping points. It may be that we have twice as many employees in the packing plants as we had in 1939, but we are marketing more than twice as many hogs. The fact that many of these men left the plants on April 1 has put the farmers in the west in a serious position, as far as marketing their hogs is concerned.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: The situation in Calgary is that they want no more men there at all. In the other plants there is some difficulty at the moment, particularly at Edmonton. We did offer to move a certain number of Japanese into this industry, but I am given to understand that this offer was refused by the industry itself. In the very tight labour situation which exists to-day, sometimes we cannot be too choosy as to the labour we may employ. Everything it is humanly possible to do is being done to face up to the labour situation in the packing plants. At the present time we are passing through a seasonal period when, by the very nature of things, there is a movement of labour from industry back to agriculture, and I can only repeat that everything possible will be done to man the packing plants in western Canada.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister a question which has to do with one or two other departments of the government as well. Agriculturists, especially in the swest, are having great difficulty in obtaining farm machinery. We questioned the Minister of Munitions and Supply in regard to the material available and were told that the Steel available now amounted to 291 per cent of the steel available in 1939. Then we had a report from the war expenditures committee to the effect that plenty of factory space is available in Canada. Therefore, it would seem that there must be a shortage of experienced labour. Would the minister tell us if he has had any demand lately for labour from the manufacturers of farm machinery, or what are the prospects of the farm implement factories obtaining sufficient labour to carry on, because the situation is much more serious now than at any time since the outbreak of war, and the prospects are that it will continue to be serious for many .months to come.

maintopic: NATIONAL SELECTIVE SERVICE MOBILIZATION REGULATIONS MEDICAL CATEGORIES
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is referring more to what we call the malleable iron industry, the foundries; that is the bottleneck. There has been a considerable movement of unskilled labour to that industry, but
